bib.title: Deep Research Agents: A Systematic Examination And Roadmap

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Deep Research Agents: A Systematic Examination and Roadmap", Yuxuan Huang, Yihang Chen, Haozheng Zhang (equal), Kang Li, Huichi Zhou, Meng Fang, Linyi Yang, Xiaoguang Li, Lifeng Shang, Songcen Xu, Jianye Hao, Kun Shao, Jun Wang (Liverpool, Huawei Noah's Ark, Oxford, UCL). arXiv:2506.18096v2 [cs.AI], 3 Sep 2025. Preprint, no venue stated. Repo: github.com/ai-agents-2030/awesome-deep-research-agent.

COVERAGE: Extracted 129,269 chars over 31 pages. Read in full: pp. 1-24 (abstract, sections 1-7, Tables 1-6, Limitation paragraph). Pp. 24-31 are the reference list (checked the start and the tail; there are no appendices). Text extraction is usable, but table cells lost their checkmark symbols (see PROBLEMS).

CLAIMS (ranked)

1. Taxonomy (the map for the note). Section 3.3 and Figure 4 give three layers.
 - Layer 1, workflow: static or dynamic.
 - Layer 2, planning strategy (dynamic only): planning-only, intent-to-planning, unified intent-planning.
 - Layer 3, agent composition (dynamic only): single-agent or multi-agent.
 - claim: Static workflows use manually predefined sequential pipelines. They are easy to implement but generalise poorly. Dynamic workflows replan from feedback.
   number: none
   setup: examples are AI Scientist (ideation, experimentation, reporting), Agent Laboratory (literature review, experimentation, synthesis) and AgentRxiv (shares intermediate results between agents).
   quote: "Static workflows rely on manually predefined task pipelines, decomposing research processes into sequential subtasks executed by dedicated agents." and "static workflows suffer from limited generalisation capabilities, as each distinct task necessitates a specifically tailored pipeline."
   where: p.10, 3.3.1
 - claim: Three planning strategies, differing in whether the user is asked to clarify.
   number: none
   setup: examples are Grok, H2O and Manus for planning-only; OpenAI DR for intent-to-planning; Gemini DR for unified intent-planning.
   quote: "The Planning-Only approach directly generates task plans based solely on initial user prompts without actively engaging in further clarification, adopted by the majority of existing DR agents, including Grok [124], H2O [39] and Manus [66]." Also: "The Intent-to-Planning strategy actively clarifies user intent prior to planning through targeted questions... utilised by OpenAI DR [78]." And: "The Unified Intent-Planning approach synthesises these methods by generating a preliminary plan from the initial prompt, together with interactively engaging the user to confirm or revise the proposed plan. Gemini DR [33]"
   where: p.12, 3.3.2
 - claim: Single-agent means one LRM does planning, tools and execution, in a ReAct-style loop. Its advantage is end-to-end RL. Its cost is heavy demand on the base model and less modularity.
   number: none
   setup: examples are Search-o1, R1-Searcher, DeepResearcher, WebDancer, WebSailor, PANGU DeepDiver, Agent-R1, ReSearch, Search-R1, WebWatcher, MiroRL, Memento, Kimi-Researcher.
   quote: "single-agent systems enable direct end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) optimisation across the entire workflow" and "this streamlined approach places significant demands on the foundation model's reasoning capabilities, contextual understanding, and autonomous selection and invocation of tools."
   where: p.12, 3.3.3
 - claim: Multi-agent means a coordinator assigns and reassigns subtasks to specialised agents. It suits parallelisable work, but coordination makes end-to-end RL hard.
   number: none
   setup: examples are OpenManus and Manus (hierarchical planner-toolcaller), OWL (manager agent plus workforce), Alita (spins up MCP servers at runtime), AWorld, WebWalker (explore-critic), WebThinker.
   quote: "a major current challenge of multi-agent systems lies in the inherent complexity of coordinating multiple independent agents, making it difficult to conduct effective end-to-end reinforcement learning optimisation."
   where: p.12

2. Retrieval (3.1): API vs browser, with a hybrid recommended.
 - claim: API-based retrieval is fast and scalable. It struggles with JavaScript-rendered content, interactive components and authentication. Browser-based retrieval reaches dynamic content but costs more latency and resources. The authors suggest hybrids.
   number: none
   quote: "While browser-based retrieval excels at capturing real-time and deeply nested content that API calls cannot reach, it also incurs greater latency, resource consumption, and complexity in handling page variability and errors, suggesting that DR agents may benefit from hybrid architectures"
   where: p.8
   setup: API examples are Gemini DR (Google Search plus arXiv APIs, "hundreds to thousands of web pages"), Grok DeepSearch, Search-o1 (Bing plus Jina Reader), DeepRetrieval (PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov), Cognitive Kernel-Pro (DuckDuckGo). Browser examples are Manus (sandboxed Chromium per session), AutoAgent (BrowserGym), DeepResearcher (browsing agent keeps a short-term memory buffer), AutoGLM Rumination. Hybrid designs: Tool-Star separates a search tool from a browser agent that returns compressed evidence; SimpleDeepSearcher uses a search-fetch-summarise loop.
 - claim: Naive RAG is a static pipeline. Agentic RAG adds iterative retrieval and still depends on pre-existing or periodically updated corpora.
   quote: "even advanced agentic RAG approaches remain constrained by their reliance on pre-existing or periodically updated corpora"
   where: p.3, 2.2
 - claim: Tool use (3.2) has three modules: code interpreter, data analytics, multimodal. MCP is the extension route.
   quote: "Most DR agents, except CoSearchAgent, embed a script execution environment." Multimodal: "most academic prototypes have not implemented it, often due to the high computational cost."
   where: p.9
 - claim: MCP is the interface to tools and A2A orchestrates agent collaboration.
   quote: "MCP serves as a standardised interface for accessing external tools, while A2A orchestrates collaborative agent interactions."
   where: p.4

3. Memory for long context (3.3.4). Three strategies.
 - claim: (i) extend the window, (ii) compress intermediate steps, (iii) external structured storage.
   number: Gemini window up to one million tokens.
   quote: "agents typically perform extensive multi-round retrieval, generating hundreds of thousands of tokens (or even millions)." Window: "Gemini model [33], which supports a context window of up to one million tokens, supplemented by a RAG setup." Window cost: "often incurs high computational costs". Compression: "a potential drawback of this approach is the loss of detailed information". Storage: "typically entail higher development and maintenance costs"
   where: pp.12-13
   setup: compression via Search-o1 "Reason-in-Documents", WebThinker auxiliary model, AI Scientist and CycleResearcher summaries. Storage via file systems (Manus, OWL, OpenManus, Avatar), vector DB (AutoAgent), knowledge graph (Agentic Reasoning), arXiv-like repository (AgentRxiv), shared KB (Agent-KB, Alita).

4. Tuning (3.4): prompt-only, then SFT, then RL, plus non-parametric.
 - claim: Prompt-only agents are capped by the base LLM. SFT methods stay tied to offline static retrieval. RL learns online query generation and tool timing.
   quote: "Although these SFT methods enhance the generalisation of deep research agents... they remain confined to offline, static retrieval pipelines" and "reinforcement learning agents acquire the ability to formulate effective search queries and determine the optimal timing for tool calls."
   where: pp.15-16
   setup: SFT works are Open-RAG, Auto-RAG, DeepRAG (binary tree search), CoRAG (rejection sampling), Li et al. hint-infer, ATLAS (trains on critical steps only).
 - claim: RL lineage is DeepRetrieval (query optimisation), ReSearch, R1-Searcher, Search-R1, Agent-R1. WebThinker uses iterative online DPO. PANGU DeepDiver uses Search Intensity Scaling with two-phase SFT then RL.
   where: p.16
 - claim: Table 3 shows three RL patterns. Open-source work mostly uses rule-based outcome rewards, GRPO or PPO, and Qwen2.5 or Llama3 bases.
   quote: "Industrial systems like Gemini DR [33] and Grok DeepSearch [124] employ proprietary RL implementations with undisclosed details, 2) Academic approaches [16, 96] favor modular RL optimization using GRPO [92] and Reinforce++ [43] with transparent reward designs, and 3) Emerging hybrid systems like SimpleDeepSearcher [100] combine process-based rewards with multi-task training across 6 QA datasets."
   where: p.16
 - claim: GRPO vs PPO, a survey assertion with no setup given.
   number: "gradient direction conflicts from 12 to 3 per training epoch"
   quote: "Empirical measurements show GRPO reduces gradient direction conflicts from 12 to 3 per training epoch, significantly accelerating convergence."
   where: pp.16-17. No citation, model, task or measurement method is given. Treat as unsupported.
 - claim: Non-parametric continual learning (3.5), mainly case-based reasoning (CBR), is the scalable alternative to weight updates. CBR works at trajectory level, unlike RAG over static text.
   quote: "agents refine their capabilities at runtime by optimising external memory, workflows, and tool configurations through continuous interaction with the external environment rather than by updating internal weights."
   where: p.17
   setup: DS-Agent, LAM, Agent K, AgentRxiv, Alita.

5. Benchmark results (Tables 4 and 5). These are compiled from papers and are not controlled comparisons.
 - Table 4 (QA, cell values lose their column labels in the extraction). Quoted rows: "DeepResearcher [135] Qwen2.5-7B-Inst 64.3 66.6 61.9 85.0 Apr-2025"; "Grok DeepSearch [124] Grok3 84.6" (column most likely GPQA; the column is not recoverable); "Search-o1 [58] QwQ-32B-preview 57.3 71.4 49.7 74.1 57.9"; "Search-R1 [52] Qwen2.5-7B-Inst 34.5 36.9 40.9 55.2". Column order is Hotpot, 2Wiki, NQ, TQ, GPQA.
   where: p.20
 - Table 5 (GAIA test): "H2O.ai DR [39] Claude3.7-Sonnet 89.25 79.87 61.22 79.73 Mar-2025", "Alita [84] ... 92.47 71.7 55.1 75.42", "Agent-KB [103] ... 75.15", "WebDancer [120] QwQ-32B 61.5 50.0 25.0 51.5". Columns are Level-1, Level-2, Level-3, Average.
   where: p.21
 - Table 5 (GAIA dev): "OpenAI DR [78] GPT-o3-customized 78.7 73.2 58.0 67.4", "Manus [66] ... 86.5 70.1 57.7 71.4", "WebThinker [59] QwQ-32B 53.8 44.2 16.7 44.7". The OpenAI DR average (67.4) is lower than all three of its level scores except Level-3, which looks inconsistent; I could not check it.
   where: p.21
 - Table 5 quirk: the H2O.ai DR row appears under test with Claude3.7-Sonnet and under dev with "h2ogpt-oasst1-512-12b", at 63.64 average.
 - claim: HLE and BrowseComp remain unsolved. Quote: "leading DR agents still exhibit suboptimal performance on the HLE and BrowserComp benchmark compared to human experts." No numbers are given. where: p.20.
 - Table 6 sizes: TriviaQA 95k, NQ 307k, HotpotQA 113k, 2Wiki 192k, SimpleQA 4.3k, Bamboogle 125, HLE 2.5k. where: p.21.

6. Industrial systems (Section 4). These are descriptive and unmeasured.
 - OpenAI DR: "single-agent architecture centred around a reinforcement learning-based, fine-tuned o3 reasoning model", with a clarification step (p.17).
 - Gemini DR: "single-agent architecture", based on Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, with a user-editable plan and an asynchronous task manager (p.18).
 - Perplexity DR: iterative search with prompt-guided model selection.
 - Grok DeepSearch: a credibility-assessment module and dynamic resource allocation.
 - Also covered: Microsoft Copilot Researcher and Analyst (o3-mini), Qwen Deep Research (Qwen3-235B-A22B), Kimi K2 (about 15.5T tokens pretraining).
 - These descriptions are vendor-derived. Note that Table 1 and Section 4.2 say Gemini DR is single-agent, while Figure 1 is drawn as multi-agent "for ease of illustration".

7. Quantified challenge claim.
 - number: "15-17% across multiple benchmarks"
 - quote: "TIR-optimised agents have demonstrated performance improvements of 15-17% across multiple benchmarks."
 - setup: citing [83] for RL with fine-grained tool rewards (tool choice, parameter accuracy, reasoning efficiency). No baseline or model is stated.
 - where: p.23.
 - Another figure: Grok DeepSearch checks consistency "through as many as seven layers of depth" (p.22).

STATED LIMITS AND OPEN CHALLENGES (Section 6, p.21 onward, and the Limitation paragraph, p.24)
- Two overarching challenges: information breadth and depth are limited by static repositories or search interfaces; execution is limited by "linear planning paradigms and monolithic agent designs".
- Broaden information sources. Browsers and search cannot reach enterprise software, apps or subscription services (example: Bloomberg Terminal). Proposed fix: modular tools via MCP, plus AI-native browsers (Browserbase, Browser Use, Fellou, Comet). Human-centred browsers cause latency, fragile locators and anti-bot problems.
- Fact checking: cross-source verification and self-reflection (Grok, Rumination, OpenAI backtracking). The text claims "dramatically lowering factual errors and hallucinations" with no measurement given.
- Asynchronous parallel execution. Quote: "most existing DR agents rely exclusively on linear task planning". Proposals: DAG task graphs and an RL-trained scheduling agent.
- Tool-integrated reasoning (TIR): SFT generalises poorly ("over-reasoning or inappropriate tool selection").
- Benchmark misalignment. Quote: "current competitive agents can often answer directly from memory, bypassing any research procedure and thus inflating their performance." Evaluations collapse research into QA and ignore the "structured, multi-modal research report". Wanted: open-web, time-sensitive, continually refreshed benchmarks and end-to-end report benchmarks. BrowseComp is cited as a step forward. Long-form sets (Qasper, ELI5) are judged ill-aligned.
- Multi-agent parametric optimisation. Quote: "current implementations predominantly utilise single-agent architectures", while multi-agent training and coordination "remains a critical open challenge". Proposed: hierarchical RL, multi-stage post-training, RL scheduler.
- Self-evolution is "underdeveloped and narrowly focused on only the case-based reasoning paradigm". Proposed: richer CBR and evolving workflows as graphs.
- Limitation paragraph, p.24: "limited generalisation across diverse tasks, inflexible task workflows, difficulty in integrating granular external tools, and substantial computational complexity associated with advanced planning and optimisation."
- Not shown: no controlled comparison of static vs dynamic or single vs multi-agent; no cost or latency numbers; no report-quality evaluation; no survey methodology (inclusion criteria, search protocol). Survey coverage stops around Aug 2025, and industry details are undisclosed.
- Conclusion framing differs from the body. The conclusion sorts methods into "prompt-based, fine-tuning-based, and reinforcement learning-based" and calls prompt-based methods "Non-parametric", while Section 3.5 uses "non-parametric" for CBR and external memory.

BUILDS ON (as printed): Wei et al. [116] chain-of-thought; ReAct [127] (Yao et al., as numbered); Toolformer [87]; WebGPT [73]; Self-RAG [7], FLARE [133]; PPO [90]; GRPO [92]; Aamodt and Plaza 1994 [1] (CBR); DS-Agent [37], Agent K [35]; Anthropic MCP and Google A2A [32]; BrowseComp [79] and GAIA [68] for evaluation.

CODE: none. The only code-like item is Figure 3's tag trace (<search>, <think>, <query>, <answer>) contrasting Search, RAG and DR on the Olympics-plus-Eurostar example (p.10).

FIGURES (not extracted with the captions tool; captions taken from the text)
- Fig 1, p.2: DR agent in a multi-agent architecture: optional planning and intent clarification, then offline retrieval (vector and relational DBs), online retrieval (APIs, browsers), analytics, coding, multimodal generation, structured report.
- Fig 2, p.4: API-based vs browser-based retrieval workflow.
- Fig 3, p.10: Search vs RAG vs Deep Research on one worked example. It shows replanning ("Impossible Tonight... Change to New plan") that RAG lacks.
- Fig 4, p.11: the taxonomy tree (static/dynamic, three planning types, single/multi-agent). This is the key figure for the note.
- Fig 5, p.18: DR agent evolution timeline.

PROBLEMS: Table 1-3 symbol cells (primary/secondary/not present, Yes/unknown, SFT/RL checkmarks) were lost in extraction, so API-vs-browser per agent and SFT-vs-RL per agent cannot be read from the tables, only from the prose. Table 4 columns are only partly recoverable (several rows show a single number with no column). Table 5 has the oddities noted above. "Kimi K2 [? ]" has an unresolved citation. The text has typos ("DeepResarcher", "BrowserComp", "Whist"). Some prose cites the wrong reference numbers: WebWatcher is [29] in the tables but [121] in the single-agent list (121 is WebWalker). No embedded instructions were found in the PDF. Figures were not inspected visually.
